| Docker | no |
| Other platforms | macOS 14 or later (x64 and arm64 .dmg and .zip); Linux x64 and arm64 (.deb, .AppImage, .tar.gz, .zip; Ubuntu 22.04+, Fedora 42+, Debian 12+; Tails and Whonix detected automatically since 2.8.0); Nix flake in the repository. No mobile apps. |
| APIs and interfaces | `gui`: Avalonia desktop GUI (wassabee.exe). Settings > Bitcoin > 'Connect to Bitcoin Node RPC' holds the node endpoint and credential string; Settings > Coordinator holds the coordinator connection string; a status-bar icon shows the Bitcoin RPC state. — authentication: Per-wallet password (applied as the BIP39 passphrase). ([documentation](https://docs.wasabiwallet.io/using-wasabi/BitcoinFullNode.html))<br>`json-rpc`: Optional JSON-RPC server: JsonRpcServerEnabled (false on mainnet, true on testnet/regtest/signet by default), JsonRpcServerPrefixes http://127.0.0.1:37128/ and http://localhost:37128/; wallet calls use the path /<WalletName>. Methods: getstatus, createwallet, recoverwallet, listwallets, loadwallet, listcoins, listunspentcoins, getwalletinfo, getnewaddress, send, build, broadcast, speeduptransaction, canceltransaction, gethistory, getfeerates, listkeys, excludefromcoinjoin, startcoinjoin, payincoinjoin, listpaymentsincoinjoin, cancelpaymentincoinjoin, startcoinjoinsweep, stopcoinjoin, buildunsafetransaction, stop. No TLS, no batching, requests processed serially; optional onion service with --rpconionenabled (new onion address at every start). — authentication: HTTP authentication with JsonRpcUser and JsonRpcPassword (random 12-character defaults generated when the default configuration is created); anonymous access is refused. 2.8.4 hardened JSON-RPC authentication (#15134). ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WasabiDoc/blob/master/docs/using-wasabi/RPC.md))<br>`cli`: Startup parameters for wassabee.exe and wassabeed.exe in the form --switch=value (case-insensitive) or environment variables WASABI_<SWITCH>. Precedence: command line, then environment, then Config.json. Overrides are not written back to Config.json. ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WasabiDoc/blob/master/docs/using-wasabi/StartupParameters.md))<br>`file`: Per-network JSON configuration in %APPDATA%\WalletWasabi\Client: Config.json (mainnet), Config.TestNet.json (testnet4), Config.RegTest.json and Config.Signet.json, all with ConfigVersion 4 since 2.8.0. The folder also holds UIConfig.json, the Wallets folder, a 'network' file naming the last network and a '.wasabi-lock' file that is held exclusively while an instance runs. An unreadable config makes Wasabi write Config.Default.json next to it and stop with an error. ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WalletWasabi/blob/v2.8.4/WalletWasabi.Client/Configuration/Serialization.cs))<br>`usb`: USB hardware wallets through the bundled HWI binary (Wasabi does not need a separately installed HWI). Documented as tested with Trezor Model T, Ledger Nano S, S Plus and X and Coldcard; the website also names Blockstream Jade and BitBox02 (BitBox02-BtcOnly since 2.0.7, BitBox02 Nova since 2.8.4). Trezor One is not supported. Hardware-wallet wallets are watch-only until the device signs over USB; they cannot take part in CoinJoin. — authentication: PIN and optional passphrase entered on the device. ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WasabiDoc/blob/master/docs/using-wasabi/ColdWasabi.md))<br>`file`: PSBT workflow (enable 'PSBT workflow' in Wallet Settings): 'Save PSBT file' for microSD signing on Coldcard; the signed -final.txn is broadcast with the Broadcaster tool. Coldcard 'Export Wallet > Wasabi Wallet' skeleton file (new-wallet.json) imports a watch-only wallet. No QR-based PSBT exchange is documented. ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WasabiDoc/blob/master/docs/using-wasabi/ColdWasabi.md))<br>`p2p`: Bitcoin P2P network: since 2.8.0 wallets download BIP158 compact block filters and blocks from P2P peers instead of a central Wasabi server, over Tor by default. ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WalletWasabi/releases/tag/v2.8.0))<br>`socks`: Bundled Tor (0.4.9.13 in 2.8.4) started and controlled by Wasabi; UseTor Enabled (default), Disabled or EnabledOnlyRunning (connect-only mode for an already-running Tor, used on Tails and Whonix). SOCKS and control ports can be set with --torsocksport and --torcontrolport, the Tor binary with --torfolder, bridges with TorBridges. ([documentation](https://github.com/WalletWasabi/WasabiDoc/blob/master/docs/using-wasabi/StartupParameters.md)) |
| Command-line interface | wassabee.exe (GUI) and wassabeed.exe (daemon) accept --network=main\|testnet\|signet\|regtest ('testnet' means testnet4 since 2.7.0), --datadir=<path>, --usetor=Enabled\|Disabled\|EnabledOnlyRunning (true/false also accepted; forced off on regtest), --torfolder, --torsocksport, --torcontrolport, --torbridges, --terminatetoronexit, --bitcoinrpcendpoint=<http://host:port> (stored in Config.json as BitcoinRpcEndPoint), --bitcoinrpccredentialstring=<rpcuser:rpcpassword or cookiefile=<path>>, --coordinatoruri, --coordinatoridentifier, --jsonrpcserverenabled, --jsonrpcuser, --jsonrpcpassword, --jsonrpcserverprefixes, --rpconionenabled, --downloadnewversion, --blockonly, --loglevel, --logmodes, --wallet=<name> (repeatable, opens wallets at start-up), --dustthreshold, --maxcoinjoinminingfeerate, --absolutemininputcount, --exchangerateprovider, --feerateestimationprovider, --externaltransactionbroadcaster, --dropunconfirmedtransactionsafterdays, --experimentalfeatures, --enablegpu, --version, --help. Environment variables WASABI_<SWITCH> (for example WASABI_NETWORK=testnet). Contrib/CLI/wcli in the repository wraps the JSON-RPC server. |
| Remote management | Only through the optional JSON-RPC server (loopback by default; optionally an onion service with --rpconionenabled). wassabeed.exe runs headless. There is no SSH or admin API. BTCortex should use only getstatus (read-only) and stop (graceful shutdown) and never call spending, CoinJoin or key-listing methods without an explicit user action. |
| Node compatibility | Optional own-node connection over Bitcoin Core JSON-RPC (Config.json keys BitcoinRpcEndPoint and BitcoinRpcCredentialString; empty by default on mainnet; testnet4 default http://localhost:48332, signet http://localhost:38332, regtest http://localhost:18443). The node is used for BIP158 filters (2.8.0 fetches them over RPC in batches, only while the node is running and synchronised; requires blockfilterindex=1 on the node), blocks, fee estimates and broadcasting; anything unavailable falls back to the default mechanisms (P2P peers, mempool.space). Credentials are 'rpcuser:rpcpassword' or a cookie file (the 2.8.4 migration code writes 'cookiefile=<path>'). Wasabi creates no wallet inside Bitcoin Core, so the removal of legacy wallets and importmulti in Core 30 does not affect it (inferred from the documented node uses). The FAQ states that pruned nodes are supported provided BIP158 filters are enabled; blocks below the prune height then come from P2P peers. 2.8.4's RPC client uses getblock with verbosity 3, which exists since Bitcoin Core 23.0 (inference). The documentation names Bitcoin Core, Bitcoin Knots and libbitcoin as full-node examples, but a Knots node at 29.4.1 or later follows a hard-forked chain and must not be wired to Wasabi. |
| Dependencies | optional: [Bitcoin Core](#entry-bitcoin-core) — Own node over RPC: server=1, blockfilterindex=1 (compatible with pruning), RPC on loopback with cookie or rpcauth credentials. Without it Wasabi uses P2P compact filters from random peers.<br>optional: [Tor (C tor daemon, Tor Expert Bundle)](#entry-tor) — Wasabi bundles and runs its own Tor by default. With UseTor=EnabledOnlyRunning it connects to an already-running Tor instead; avoid two Tor instances competing for the same SOCKS/control ports.<br>enhances: [HWI (Hardware Wallet Interface)](#entry-hwi) — HWI ships inside Wasabi (2.0.8 updated it to 3.0.0, 2.3.0 to 3.1.0); BTCortex does not need to install it for Wasabi.<br>optional: [COLDCARD](#entry-coldcard) or [Trezor (Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3, Model T, Model One)](#entry-trezor) or [Ledger (Nano S Plus, Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax)](#entry-ledger) or [BitBox02 (BitBox02 and BitBox02 Nova, Multi and Bitcoin-only editions)](#entry-bitbox02) or [Blockstream Jade](#entry-jade) — Hardware wallets via HWI over USB, or Coldcard via PSBT files on microSD. CoinJoin is not possible with hardware-wallet keys. |
| Networking | Outbound only by default and routed through Tor: Bitcoin P2P peers (filters and blocks), mempool.space (ExchangeRateProvider, FeeRateEstimationProvider and ExternalTransactionBroadcaster all default to MempoolSpace), the user-selected CoinJoin coordinator (CoordinatorUri is empty by default since zkSNACKs closed) and update checks (DownloadNewVersion true by default). Optional Bitcoin Core RPC (for example http://127.0.0.1:8332). Optional JSON-RPC listener on 127.0.0.1:37128 (off by default on mainnet). Bundled Tor uses local SOCKS and control ports chosen by Wasabi unless overridden. No inbound ports otherwise. |
| Storage | Installer about 99 MB and ZIP about 96 MB (2.8.4). The size of the data directory (headers, filter cache, wallets, logs) was not measured. 2.8.0 added wallet-birthday checkpoints and a filter checkpoint at height 950 000, so new wallets skip earlier history. |
| Resources | Not documented. GPU rendering is on by default (EnableGpu). The daemon wassabeed.exe is described as minimising CPU, GPU, memory and bandwidth use. |
| Security implications | Privacy relies on Tor plus client-side filtering; the documentation strongly advises against disabling Tor. CoinJoin needs a third-party coordinator that the user chooses: since 2.2.0 the client only joins rounds without a coordination fee and pays only mining fees, the coordinator sets the round's mining fee rate (capped by MaxCoinJoinMiningFeeRate, default 50) and may receive decomposition leftovers of up to 10 000 sats; WabiSabi prevents the coordinator from linking inputs to outputs, but it sees registered inputs and can ban them. BTCortex must never pick a coordinator. JSON-RPC has no TLS, some methods work without the wallet password because the wallet file is readable, and send/startcoinjoin carry passwords in request bodies: keep it disabled unless needed and never log its traffic. Release verification: per-file .asc and SHA256SUMS.asc signed with the zkSNACKs OpenPGP key 6FB3 872B 5D42 292F 5992 0797 8563 4832 8949 861E (RSA-2048, 'zkSNACKs <zksnacks@gmail.com>', valid until 2028-02-24; PGP.txt in the repository), still used for 2.8.x per the installation guide; the MSI is Authenticode-signed (Lucas Ontivero). 2.8.4 deprecates the 'compatibility passphrase' feature (users seeing its warning should create a new wallet) and ignores headers from longer chains with less accumulated work. Legal context (neutral): zkSNACKs blocked US persons from its websites and products in April 2024 and stopped coordinating on 2024-06-01 citing the need for more legal certainty; whether operating or using a CoinJoin coordinator is regulated depends on the jurisdiction (compare the 2025 US convictions of the Samourai Wallet founders for conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business). |
| Licence | MIT |
| Licence notes | MIT (LICENSE.md; NOTICE.md lists third-party components). The packages bundle Tor and HWI binaries under their own licences. Redistribution is allowed; downloading the official artefacts at install time avoids bundling them in BTCortex. |
| Integration mechanisms | Download Wasabi-<version>-win-x64.zip (or the MSI) and its .asc from the GitHub release; verify the OpenPGP signature against the pinned fingerprint 6FB3872B5D42292F59920797856348328949861E (optionally also SHA256SUMS.asc), then the SHA-256<br>Zero-touch install without elevation: extract the ZIP into a versioned per-user directory under %LOCALAPPDATA% and create BTCortex-owned shortcuts<br>Unattended MSI alternative (needs elevation): msiexec /i Wasabi-<version>.msi /qn /norestart; per-machine install to C:\Program Files\WasabiWallet\; MajorUpgrade replaces older versions and refuses downgrades<br>Managed launch with documented startup parameters: wassabee.exe --network=main --bitcoinrpcendpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8332 --bitcoinrpccredentialstring=cookiefile=<Core data directory>\.cookie --downloadnewversion=false (parameters are not persisted)<br>Persistent pre-configuration only while Wasabi is closed (the '.wasabi-lock' file in %APPDATA%\WalletWasabi\Client must not be locked): read Config.json, require ConfigVersion 4, set BitcoinRpcEndPoint and BitcoinRpcCredentialString, keep every other key, write atomically and keep a backup<br>Prepare the managed node: blockfilterindex=1 (works with pruning) and server=1, then wait for getindexinfo to report the basic block filter index as synced<br>Leave CoordinatorUri empty and explain in the UI that CoinJoin requires a coordinator chosen by the user<br>Health and shutdown: process and lock-file detection; JSON-RPC getstatus and stop only if the user enabled the JSON-RPC server<br>Detect existing installations: MSI UpgradeCode {D8E80773-D8CF-4031-B8B3-AA750AF0B413}, C:\Program Files\WasabiWallet\wassabee.exe and %APPDATA%\WalletWasabi\Client |
| Feasible support levels | Fully Managed, Connected Application, External Launcher |
| Recommended support level | Fully Managed |
| Implementation feasibility | medium — Official, OpenPGP-verifiable x64 ZIP and MSI; documented startup parameters override Config.json without modifying it, so BTCortex can launch Wasabi wired to the managed node and with its own updater disabled. Persisted pre-configuration means editing Config.json while Wasabi is closed: the decoder is strict (an unreadable file stops start-up) and the schema changed in 2.6.0 (BackendUri, UseBitcoinRpc), 2.7.0 (per-network files) and 2.8.0 (ConfigVersion 4, no indexer URI), so the writer must be version-gated; the public FAQ still shows the older UseBitcoinRpc key. CoinJoin depends on a user-chosen third-party coordinator and carries jurisdiction-dependent legal questions, which BTCortex must surface rather than decide. P2 because Wasabi is an optional privacy wallet, not part of the essential Phase 5 integrations; it does work with the pruned test node once blockfilterindex=1 is set (FAQ statement, not tested). |
| Priority | P2 |
| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | History: Wasabi 1.x (zkSNACKs, Tor plus ZeroLink CoinJoin) is superseded by 2.x (WabiSabi). 2.0.8 (2024-06-01) added custom coordinators, Tor bridges and Tails/Whonix connect-only mode after the zkSNACKs coordinator shut down. 2.6.0 was the first version to synchronise without a central server. 2.7.0 (2025-08-30) stopped bundling bitcoind binaries, introduced per-network config files and Bitcoin RPC endpoints (including onion RPC) and made full RBF the default. 2.8.0 (2026-06-27) introduced P2P compact-filter synchronisation, wallet-birthday checkpoints, paying inside a CoinJoin, payment batching, sub-1 sat/vB fees, signet, an experimental Scheme scripting language and .NET 10. On 2026-10-21 master removed the remaining indexer ('Remove Indexer (#15190)'), so the next release is expected to drop it entirely. Supported standards listed by the documentation: BIP21, 32, 38, 39, 44, 72, 78 (Payjoin), 84, 86, 125, 141, 143, 144, 157, 158, 173, 174, 341 and 352 (sending to Silent Payments; receiving 'coming soon'), plus SLIP-39; BIP37 and BIP69 are explicitly not supported. No multisig, no miniscript, no BIP329 label export documented, no QR PSBT exchange. |

**Requires verification**

- The zkSNACKs announcement on blog.wasabiwallet.io could not be fetched (the host did not resolve on 2026-10-21); the shutdown date and stated reason come from the v2.0.8 release notes and NoBS Bitcoin.
- The format accepted for cookie authentication ('cookiefile=<path>') is inferred from the 2.8.4 migration code and NBitcoin conventions; it was not tested, nor whether Wasabi re-reads a rotated cookie after a node restart.
- Whether 'msiexec /qn' installs Wasabi completely without the WixUI_InstallDir dialogs was not tested.
- The purpose and verification key of SHA256SUMS.wasabisig (presumably for the in-app updater) were not verified.
- Whether the ZIP's wassabee.exe is Authenticode-signed was not checked; only the MSI signature is documented.
- The HWI version bundled with 2.8.4 was not verified (BitBox02 Nova support suggests HWI 3.2.0).
- The minimum Bitcoin Core version for the RPC connection is not documented; Core 23.0 or later is inferred from the use of getblock verbosity 3.
- Behaviour with a pruned BTCortex node (filters via RPC, older blocks from P2P peers) was not tested; the FAQ only states that pruned nodes are supported.
- The exact semantics of UseTor=EnabledOnlyRunning with a BTCortex-managed Tor (control-port authentication) were not verified.

Latest commits 2026-10-15 (signature audit refactor, PR #517 from an Unchained contributor). Docker Hub caravanbitcoin/coordinator:1.19.2 pushed 2026-07-20. |
| Superseded by | — |

| Windows versions | Not stated upstream; any Windows version that runs a current Chromium-based browser (direct device access relies on browser USB APIs) |

| Windows distribution | No Windows package. Options: the hosted site (caravanmultisig.com; also linked: caravan-bitcoin.github.io/caravan and caravan-coordinator.vercel.app), the official Docker image caravanbitcoin/coordinator (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64; container port 80), or a static build from source with Node.js >= 24 and npm >= 11.10 (npm run build:coordinator). |
| WSL2 | likely |
| Docker | official-image |
| Other platforms | Any operating system with a modern browser; npm libraries @caravan/bitcoin, @caravan/psbt, @caravan/wallets, @caravan/clients, @caravan/multisig for developers. |
| APIs and interfaces | `http`: Static single-page application with hash routing (for example http://localhost:8000/#), served by the hosted sites, the Docker image (nginx, container port 80) or vite (preview 4173, development 5173). ([documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/caravan-bitcoin/caravan/main/apps/coordinator/README.md))<br>`json-rpc`: Private client: Bitcoin Core JSON-RPC called from the browser (axios POST, HTTP basic auth, no timeout) through a CORS-adding reverse proxy (upstream nginx template: listen 8080, proxy to 127.0.0.1:8332). Uses an optional walletName for a watch-only descriptor wallet that the user creates (createwallet blank=true disable_private_keys=true load_on_startup=true). Calls importdescriptors (timestamp "now", or 0 when a rescan is requested), getwalletinfo, listunspent, gettransaction, getreceivedbyaddress, listtransactions, getmempoolentry, estimatesmartfee, getrawtransaction and sendrawtransaction. — authentication: RPC user and password sent as HTTP basic authentication from the browser ([documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/caravan-bitcoin/caravan/main/apps/coordinator/README.md))<br>`rest`: Public client: Esplora-style APIs at https://unchained.mempool.space (default) or https://blockstream.info: /address/{a}/utxo, /address/{a}, /address/{a}/txs, /tx/{txid}, /tx/{txid}/hex, POST /tx, /v1/fees/recommended, /v1/mining/blocks/fee-rates/all, /fee-estimates; mainnet and testnet only. ([documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/caravan-bitcoin/caravan/main/packages/caravan-clients/src/client.ts))<br>`usb`: Direct keystores from the browser: Trezor (@trezor/transport; the README still says Trezor Bridge is required), Ledger and Ledger v2 (wallet policy registration with policy HMACs), BitBox and Jade (metadata, xpub export, multisig signing, address confirmation, policy registration where supported). — authentication: On-device confirmation ([documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/caravan-bitcoin/caravan/main/packages/caravan-wallets/src/index.ts))<br>`qr`: BC-UR 2 (BCUR2 keystore, 1.19.0+) for xpub import, PSBT signing, wallet registration and address confirmation with QR signers. ([documentation](https://github.com/caravan-bitcoin/caravan/releases.atom))<br>`file`: Wallet configuration JSON (MultisigWalletConfig: name, uuid, quorum.requiredSigners and totalSigners, addressType, extendedPublicKeys[] with xfp, bip32Path and xpub, network, ledgerPolicyHmacs[]); indirect signing for Coldcard, Hermit and custom keys through files or text; PSBT import and export. ([documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/caravan-bitcoin/caravan/main/packages/multisig/src/types.ts)) |
| Command-line interface | — |
| Remote management | Nothing to manage: the coordinator is stateless. A node on another machine can serve as the private client only through an authenticated, CORS-restricted HTTPS proxy; an SSH tunnel or a private network is preferable to exposing RPC. |
| Node compatibility | Private client: Bitcoin Core with RPC and wallets enabled, a user-created watch-only descriptor wallet and a reverse proxy that adds CORS headers (Bitcoin Core sends none). Only descriptor-wallet RPCs are used by the client (a legacy importmulti helper remains in bitcoind.ts but the client calls importdescriptors), so the code path is compatible with Core 30.x and 31.1. txindex is not required for wallet transactions. The README says users must re-index when an imported wallet's history predates the import and txindex is off; a descriptor rescan (timestamp 0) normally suffices on an unpruned node, while a pruned node cannot serve history below its prune height. Regtest only through the private client with an uploaded configuration. Public client: Unchained's mempool.space instance or Blockstream's Esplora. Bitcoin Knots >= 29.4.1 follows a different chain. |
| Dependencies | requires: [Bitcoin Core](#entry-bitcoin-core) or [mempool.space public API](#entry-mempool-space-api) or [blockstream.info Esplora API](#entry-blockstream-info-api) — A private Bitcoin Core node behind a CORS proxy, or a public Esplora/mempool API (unchained.mempool.space by default).<br>enhances: [Trezor (Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3, Model T, Model One)](#entry-trezor) or [Ledger (Nano S Plus, Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax)](#entry-ledger) or [BitBox02 (BitBox02 and BitBox02 Nova, Multi and Bitcoin-only editions)](#entry-bitbox02) or [Blockstream Jade](#entry-jade) or [COLDCARD](#entry-coldcard) — Keystores in @caravan/wallets; QR signers through BC-UR 2. |
| Networking | Served from whatever origin hosts it (hosted HTTPS sites, Docker nginx on container port 80, vite 4173/5173). The browser calls unchained.mempool.space or blockstream.info in public mode, or the user's CORS proxy in private mode (upstream example: http://localhost:8080 for a node on 127.0.0.1:8332). Device libraries may contact vendor services (not checked). |
| Storage | Stateless: Caravan 'does not itself store any data'; the user must keep the wallet configuration file and the addresses, redeem scripts and BIP32 paths it creates. In private mode the watch-only descriptor wallet lives in Bitcoin Core. |
| Resources | Negligible at run time (static web application). Building from source needs Node.js >= 24 and npm >= 11.10. |
| Security implications | Caravan holds no keys; signatures are produced on devices or by external signers after explicit user action. Loading the coordinator from a hosted origin means trusting remote JavaScript that sees xpubs and, in private mode, the node's RPC credentials; a locally served copy is preferable. The CORS proxy must allow only the Caravan origin and RPC must stay on loopback; the README stresses that CORS headers 'are essential to protecting the security of your coins'. Public mode reveals every wallet address to the API operator (Unchained's mempool.space instance or Blockstream). Supply-chain hardening: a 7-day npm min-release-age in .npmrc. |
| Licence | MIT |
| Licence notes | MIT ('Copyright (c) 2024 Caravan'); BTCortex may serve a built copy with the notice. |
| Integration mechanisms | Open the hosted coordinator or a locally served build in the user's Chromium-based browser (external launcher); do not embed it in BTCortex's WebView2 until WebHID/WebUSB device access has been tested there<br>Optionally run the official caravanbitcoin/coordinator image on loopback (managed Docker) or serve the static build from BTCortex's sidecar<br>Generate a Caravan wallet configuration JSON from xpubs or a sortedmulti descriptor that BTCortex already holds (watch-only)<br>For private mode: create the watch-only descriptor wallet with load_on_startup=true and a dedicated rpcauth user with an rpcwhitelist limited to the RPCs Caravan uses, and expose them through a loopback CORS proxy restricted to the Caravan origin |
| Feasible support levels | External Launcher, Managed via Docker, Connected Application, Research Only |
| Recommended support level | External Launcher |
| Implementation feasibility | medium — Caravan is maintained and MIT-licensed but has no Windows artefact: it is a static web application reached through a hosted site, a Docker image or a source build. Private-node mode needs a CORS proxy and RPC credentials in the browser, which BTCortex would have to provide carefully. Launching it (with a generated wallet configuration file) is easy; full private-node wiring is a later step. Priority P3. |
| Priority | P3 |
| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | Multisig only. Hermit (Unchained's shard-based signer) is supported as an indirect keystore. PSBTv2 handling was fixed in @caravan/psbt 2.1.1. No miniscript, Taproot multisig or BIP329 label support was found. The repository moved from unchained-capital/caravan to caravan-bitcoin/caravan and the libraries were renamed from unchained-bitcoin and unchained-wallets to @caravan/bitcoin and @caravan/wallets. |

([documentation](https://nunchuk.io/))<br>`file`: PSBT files and wallet configuration export as output descriptors or BSMS (BIP129); microSD workflows for air-gapped signers such as Coldcard. The wallet 'nunchuk' is created without load_on_startup, so on a pruned node it can fall behind pruning while Nunchuk is closed; rescanblockchain cannot reach below the prune height. Optional SOCKS5 proxy (Tor) for Electrum connections. |
| Storage | Settings in the Windows registry: QSettings NativeFormat, user scope, organisation 'nunchuk', application 'NunchukClient' (HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\nunchuk\NunchukClient). Keys are stored unprefixed for guests and as <group>/<key> when a group is set; primaryServer, isStarted and mainnetList are always unprefixed. The mainnet server key is spelt mainnestServer. Wallet data under QStandardPaths::AppDataLocation (expected %APPDATA%\nunchuk\NunchukClient); optional database encryption (enableDBEncryption, default false). In Bitcoin Core: one watch-only wallet named nunchuk. |
| Resources | Not documented. Qt 6 including Qt WebEngine (Chromium) in the bundle. |
| Security implications | The default Electrum server is operated by Nunchuk and learns the wallet's addresses: point Nunchuk at the user's own server. Nunchuk can create software keys (stored by the app; database encryption is off by default): BTCortex must not collect, back up or transmit them. Paid assisted, inheritance and group features involve Nunchuk-operated services and an account (key arrangements per plan not verified). Windows binaries are not Authenticode-signed; SHA256SUMS.asc is produced by a CI workflow with a key held as a GitHub secret (release notes link key 8C8ECD3F660CA53CD878792A6E38A462ED2EF525 on keys.openpgp.org); Windows and macOS reproducible builds are not yet independently verifiable. The bundled HWI comes from a non-upstream fork. Core RPC credentials are stored in the registry. Unpinned self-signed Electrum certificates are accepted with a warning. |

| Licence notes | The README states GNU GPL v3 (libnunchuk is GPL v3 as well); whether -only or -or-later applies was not checked. Redistribution requires offering the source. Nunchuk's subscription services have their own terms. |

| Feasible support levels | External Launcher, Connected Application, Research Only |
| Recommended support level | External Launcher |

Pre-configuration is the weak point: settings live in the registry under undocumented keys that move under a group prefix once the user signs in, Core RPC needs a password (no cookie), and the default server is Nunchuk's own. BTCortex should install, verify and launch Nunchuk and present the connection values for the user to enter; registry pre-seeding stays research-only until tested. Priority P2. |

### Specter Desktop

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | Multisignature coordinators |
| Purpose | Python/Flask wallet coordinator with an Electron desktop shell that uses Bitcoin Core (or an Electrum server through its bundled Spectrum adapter) as a watch-only back end for single-signature and multisignature wallets whose keys stay on hardware wallets and air-gapped signers. PSBTs travel to the devices over USB (bundled HWI library), animated QR codes or SD-card files. |
| Official website | <https://specter.solutions/> |
| Official repository | <https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop> |
| Maintenance status | active — Stable v2.1.11 published 2026-08-09 (v2.1.10 2026-06-29, v2.1.9 2026-05-18, v2.1.8 2026-04-30, v2.1.7 April 2026); prerelease v2.2.0-pre5 published 2026-08-15. Latest master commit 2026-09-03 (#2702, Specter-DIY xpub import); repository pushed 2026-10-20, not archived, 253 open issues. No maintenance-mode or discontinuation announcement was found. The 2026 releases consist mostly of dependency, CI (move to GitHub Actions) and security fixes; the documentation's release-notes page stops at v2.1.0 (2025-01-03) and upstream CI tests bitcoind 27.2.0 (v2.1.8 notes). |

| Verification date | 2026-10-21 |
| Native Windows | yes |
| Windows versions | Not stated upstream; the GUI is built on Electron 39 (package.json ^39.8.10), which implies 64-bit Windows 10 or later |
| Windows architectures | x64 |
| Windows distribution | Specter-Setup-v2.1.11.exe (97 867 547 bytes): electron-builder NSIS installer whose build configuration sets no Windows options, so electron-builder defaults apply (one-click, per-user, no elevation); the release notes say the GUI bundles the Specter server. specterd-v2.1.11-win64.zip (72 546 815 bytes): PyInstaller command-line server only, serving the same web UI. No portable GUI. The build configuration contains no Windows code-signing settings. Checksums in SHA256SUMS, signed in SHA256SUMS.asc. |
| WSL2 | likely |
| Docker | official-image |
| Other platforms | macOS 10.15 or later (.dmg, not notarised) and specterd for macOS arm64/x64; Linux x86_64 GUI tarball and specterd ZIP (udev rules included); PyPI package cryptoadvance.specter (python -m cryptoadvance.specter server); Docker images published to GitHub Container Registry per release (images before v2.1.2 came from third parties); used on node platforms (Umbrel and RaspiBlitz users appear in the issue tracker). |
| APIs and interfaces | `http`: Flask web UI, by default on http://127.0.0.1:25441 (HOST/PORT environment variables or --host/--port). Optional TLS with --cert/--key or a generated self-signed certificate (--ssl). REST API (liveness, readyness, specter object, full transaction list, wallet and PSBT endpoints) enabled with SPECTER_API_ACTIVE=True. The Electron shell only embeds this UI. — authentication: config.json auth.method defaults to "none" (no login); password-only and username/password modes exist. REST API protected through Flask-HTTPAuth and API tokens (2.1.11 validates active tokens). Flask session protection "strong" by default; ProductionConfig generates a random SECRET_KEY per start unless SECRET_KEY is set. ([documentation](https://docs.specter.solutions/desktop/api/))<br>`json-rpc`: Client of Bitcoin Core JSON-RPC. With autodetect=true it re-reads bitcoin.conf and the .cookie file of the configured data directory on every connection; otherwise it uses host, port, protocol, user and password from the node file. For each Specter wallet it creates a watch-only descriptor wallet specter/<alias> (createwallet with disable_private_keys=true, blank=true, passphrase "", avoid_reuse=false, descriptors=true when Core >= 0.21) and imports xpub descriptors with importdescriptors (timestamp "now", watchonly); importmulti is used only for legacy wallets on nodes older than 0.21. The connection test calls getnetworkinfo (warns below version 200000) and listwallets ("Wallets disabled"). — authentication: Cookie (autodetect) or rpcuser/rpcpassword stored in plain text in the node JSON file ([documentation](https://docs.specter.solutions/desktop/connect-your-node/))<br>`electrum-protocol`: Optional Spectrum adapter (cryptoadvance.spectrum 0.8.0, bundled as the "spectrum" extension, node alias spectrum_node) that emulates the Bitcoin Core RPC API on top of an Electrum server (persisted keys host, port, ssl) and caches wallet data in SQLite at <data folder>\sqlite\db.sqlite. Uses Specter's SOCKS proxy when Tor is configured. Spectrum's README lists open limitations (no reconnection after a disconnect, keypool not refilled, no RPC credentials). ([documentation](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/spectrum))<br>`usb`: USB hardware wallets through the bundled HWI Python library (hwi 3.1.0 since v2.1.10): device classes ColdCard, Trezor, Ledger, BitBox02, Keepkey, Jade and Specter (DIY). The HWI bridge mode (--hwibridge) lets a remote Specter server reach devices plugged into the local machine through the browser. — authentication: PIN and passphrase entry happen on or for the device; HWI bridge settings protected with authentication and CSRF since 2.1.11 ([documentation](https://docs.specter.solutions/desktop/hwibridge/))<br>`qr`: QR signers handled through the browser (display and webcam scanning): device classes Keystone, Cobo, Passport, SeedSigner (taproot_support, animated at 2 frames per second, QR message signing) and Specter DIY; wallet export to Jade by QR was added in 2.1.0. ([documentation](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/blob/master/src/cryptoadvance/specter/devices/seedsigner.py))<br>`file`: JSON state in the Specter data folder (config.json, nodes\<alias>.json with a python_class field, wallet and device JSON files), PSBT and wallet export/import files, SD-card signers (sd_card_device base class), and a backup ZIP (Settings > Backup Specter). ([documentation](https://docs.specter.solutions/desktop/faq/))<br>`cli`: specterd server [options] (see the cli field). The Electron shell starts specterd as 'server --no-filelog' plus the space-separated specterdCLIArgs from app_settings.json and waits up to 180 s for 'Serving Flask app' on stdout. ([documentation](https://docs.specter.solutions/desktop/daemon/))<br>`gui`: Electron desktop application (Specter-Setup-*.exe) that starts the bundled specterd and shows the web UI, or connects to a remote Specter server (mode and specterURL in app_settings.json). — authentication: Optional HTTP basic authentication towards a remote Specter (basicAuth, basicAuthUser, basicAuthPass in app_settings.json) ([documentation](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/releases/tag/v2.1.11)) |
| Command-line interface | specterd.exe server [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 25441] [--cert <file> --key <file> \| --ssl/--no-ssl] [--debug/--no-debug] [--filelog/--no-filelog] [--tor] [--hwibridge] [--skiphwiinitialisation] [--devstatus-threshold alpha\|beta\|prod] [--specter-data-folder <dir>] [--config <class in config.py, default ProductionConfig>]. Environment: SPECTER_DATA_FOLDER (default ~/.specter), SPECTER_CONFIG, HOST, PORT, CONNECT_TOR, SECRET_KEY, SPECTER_API_ACTIVE, BITCOIN_RPC_TIMEOUT (60 s in ProductionConfig), and since 2.1.7 BTC_RPC_USER, BTC_RPC_PASSWORD, BTC_RPC_HOST, BTC_RPC_PORT, BTC_RPC_PROTOCOL, which create an external node named "Bitcoin Core" (autodetect off) when no node exists yet. pip installs: python -m cryptoadvance.specter server. |
| Remote management | Specter is itself a web application. Remote use needs a non-loopback bind (--host 0.0.0.0 exposes the UI to the LAN; only with authentication and TLS), an SSH tunnel or reverse proxy (documented), or a Tor hidden service (--tor or the Tor settings page; the FAQ says hidden-service mode is not supported in 2.0 while the 2.1.x server code still starts one). The REST API's liveness and readyness endpoints suit health checks. With a remote Specter, USB devices are reached through the HWI bridge running on the user's machine. |
| Node compatibility | Bitcoin Core with RPC enabled and wallets enabled (disablewallet=0; the FAQ says txindex is not required). Version checks: getnetworkinfo version >= 200000 expected, descriptor wallets from 0.21 (210000), Taproot from 22.0. The 2.1.0 notes state compatibility with Core 28.0; CI tests bitcoind 27.2.0. Core 30.x/31.1: no upstream statement, but the 0.21+ code path uses only descriptor-wallet RPCs (createwallet descriptors=true, importdescriptors), none of which were removed in 30.0, and an issue reporter (#2624) ran Specter 2.1.8 against Core 30.2. Specter wallets created as legacy (BDB) wallets on old nodes cannot be loaded by Core 30+ without Core's migratewallet. Wallets are created without load_on_startup, so they are not loaded when Core starts without Specter. Autodetect: the Windows default data directory is %APPDATA%\Bitcoin only (Core 28+ defaults to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bitcoin), the network is taken from testnet=1, signet=1 or regtest=1 in bitcoin.conf (otherwise main), and cookies are looked up in the main, testnet3, regtest and signet folders; testnet4 is not supported (#2516 open). Pruned nodes: new wallets work; full-history rescans need the blocks, and the UTXO-only scan works on pruned nodes but queries a user-configured block explorer for transaction data. Electrum servers (Fulcrum, electrs, ElectrumX) through Spectrum. Bitcoin Knots >= 29.4.1 follows a different chain and must not be pre-wired silently. |
| Dependencies | requires: [Bitcoin Core](#entry-bitcoin-core) or [Fulcrum](#entry-fulcrum) or [electrs (Electrum Rust Server)](#entry-electrs) or [ElectrumX](#entry-electrumx) — Either a Bitcoin Core node over RPC (wallets enabled, cookie or rpcauth) or an Electrum server through the bundled Spectrum adapter.<br>requires: [HWI (Hardware Wallet Interface)](#entry-hwi) — Bundled as a Python library (hwi==3.1.0 pinned in requirements since v2.1.10); BTCortex must not install HWI separately for Specter. Additions of HWI 3.2.0 (Jade Plus, BitBox02 Nova, testnet4) are therefore not part of Specter's USB path.<br>optional: [Tor (C tor daemon, Tor Expert Bundle)](#entry-tor) — tor_type "custom" with proxy_url socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050 (and only_tor) routes outbound requests through BTCortex's Tor. tor_type "builtin" makes Specter install and run its own Tor daemon under <data folder>\tor-binaries, which BTCortex should avoid.<br>enhances: [COLDCARD](#entry-coldcard) or [Trezor (Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3, Model T, Model One)](#entry-trezor) or [Ledger (Nano S Plus, Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax)](#entry-ledger) or [BitBox02 (BitBox02 and BitBox02 Nova, Multi and Bitcoin-only editions)](#entry-bitbox02) or [Blockstream Jade](#entry-jade) or [KeepKey](#entry-keepkey) or [Specter DIY](#entry-specter-diy) or [Keystone](#entry-keystone) or [Foundation Passport](#entry-passport) or [SeedSigner](#entry-seedsigner) — Device types registered in Specter: HWI USB devices plus QR and SD-card signers. |
| Networking | Listens on 127.0.0.1:25441 by default (HTTP; HTTPS with --cert/--key or --ssl); --host 0.0.0.0 exposes it to the LAN. Outbound: Bitcoin Core RPC (8332, 18332, 38332 or 18443 by network) or an Electrum server through Spectrum; optional SOCKS proxy (proxy_url default socks5h://localhost:9050, only_tor false); fee estimation (fee_estimator "bitcoin_core" by default, custom URL possible); price check (off by default); a user-configured block explorer for the UTXO scan (explorers empty by default); extension services (for example the Swan integration) when used. If its bundled specterd binary is missing or fails the pinned hash, the Electron shell downloads https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/releases/download/<version>/specterd-<version>-win64.zip. |
| Storage | Data folder %USERPROFILE%\.specter (os.path.expanduser('~/.specter'); override with SPECTER_DATA_FOLDER or --specter-data-folder): config.json (global settings), nodes\<alias>.json, wallet and device JSON files, sqlite\db.sqlite (Spectrum cache), specterApp.log, app_settings.json (Electron shell), .tor_service_key and onion.txt (hidden service), tor-binaries\ (built-in Tor). JSON writes rename the old file to .bkp, write and re-read for verification (not atomic, in-process lock only). In Bitcoin Core: one watch-only descriptor wallet per Specter wallet under <walletdir>\specter\<alias>. Sizes are not documented; the installer is about 98 MB. |
| Resources | Not documented upstream. Two processes when the GUI is used (Electron shell and the PyInstaller specterd); Spectrum adds an SQLite cache and its own Electrum synchronisation. |
| Security implications | Watch-only by default: keys stay on devices and PSBTs are signed on the device after explicit confirmation. However, Specter also offers a "Bitcoin Core (hot wallet)" device type that takes a mnemonic and imports xprv descriptors into a Core wallet under _hotstorage (protected only by an optional wallet passphrase); BTCortex must never create, pre-configure or recommend it. Authentication is off by default and the data folder (including node passwords and xpubs) is not encrypted at rest (warning added in 2.1.11). 2026 security fixes: open-redirect bypass (2.1.7), warning for known default secret keys (2.1.7), HWI bridge settings protected by auth and CSRF, API token validation and a ColdCard Mk3 seed-entropy advisory warning (2.1.11). Release verification: SHA256SUMS signed with the "Specter Signer 2026" OpenPGP key 9DC3 3CA8 3058 9DE3 B322 5C26 EEF5 756B 2EA4 2349 (signed by k9ert's key, published on keyserver.ubuntu.com). The Electron fallback download checks the extracted specterd against a pinned SHA-256 but not OpenPGP. The UTXO scan contacts an external block explorer (privacy). |
| Licence | MIT |
| Licence notes | MIT (repository licence). Bundled extensions and dependencies carry their own licences (HWI is MIT; others not checked). Downloading the official release at install time avoids redistribution questions. |
| Integration mechanisms | Download specterd-v<version>-win64.zip (or Specter-Setup-v<version>.exe) with SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.asc from the GitHub release; verify the OpenPGP signature against the pinned fingerprint 9DC33CA830589DE3B3225C26EEF5756B2EA42349, then the SHA-256 of the artefact<br>Preferred zero-touch form: extract specterd into a per-user versioned folder and run it as a supervised child process: specterd.exe server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 25441 --no-filelog (capture stdout/stderr), then open http://127.0.0.1:25441 in the user's browser or a BTCortex window<br>GUI form: run Specter-Setup-v<version>.exe /S (electron-builder NSIS convention, per-user, no elevation; to be tested) and launch it from the Start menu<br>While Specter is stopped, write %USERPROFILE%\.specter\nodes\<alias>.json (python_class cryptoadvance.specter.node.Node, name, alias, autodetect true, datadir = managed Core data directory, host localhost, port 8332, protocol http, node_type BTC, fullpath) and set active_node_alias in config.json; alternatively start specterd once with BTC_RPC_USER, BTC_RPC_PASSWORD, BTC_RPC_HOST, BTC_RPC_PORT and BTC_RPC_PROTOCOL for a dedicated rpcauth user (2.1.7+)<br>While Specter is stopped, set tor_type "custom", proxy_url "socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050", tor_control_port "" and optionally only_tor true in config.json when BTCortex's Tor runs<br>After Specter creates specter/<alias>, keep it loaded at node start (wallet=specter/<alias> in bitcoin.conf or a load with load_on_startup=true), which matters on pruned nodes<br>Health checks: REST liveness/readyness endpoints (API enabled) or HTTP 200 on the UI, plus process supervision<br>Detect existing installations: %USERPROFILE%\.specter, the per-user Electron install, specterd.exe/Specter.exe processes and port 25441<br>Run the official container image or the Linux specterd in WSL2 when the node runs there; connect to Specter on node platforms as a remote web application<br>Never create or import a 'Bitcoin Core (hot wallet)' device and never ask for mnemonics |
| Feasible support levels | Connected Application, Fully Managed, External Launcher, Managed via Docker, Managed via WSL2, Remote Managed |
| Recommended support level | Connected Application |
| Implementation feasibility | medium — specterd-win64.zip is a verifiable portable artefact and the node connection lives in JSON files that BTCortex can write while Specter is stopped, so Specter can be pre-wired to the managed node without user input. Caveats: the file formats are internal (not documented as an interface), autodetect knows only %APPDATA%\Bitcoin as the Windows default and selects the network from testnet=1/signet=1/regtest=1 in bitcoin.conf (not from -chain or chain=), testnet4 is unsupported, Specter's Core wallets are not loaded at node start-up, authentication is off by default, HWI is pinned at 3.1.0, and Core 30/31 are not covered by upstream CI. Priority P2: specification section 8 names the Core -> Specter -> hardware wallet flow, but Sparrow covers the same need with fewer moving parts; a fully-managed level for specterd is feasible later. |
| Priority | P2 |
| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | Specter 2.0 removed the Specter-managed internal bitcoind, so it does not compete with BTCortex's node. Bundled extensions: Spectrum, timelock recovery (specterext-timelockrecovery 0.2.3), exfund, faucet, stacktrack and the Liquid issuer; Liquid/Elements is supported. The FAQ limits multisig address types to nested and native SegWit; no miniscript wallet support was found. BIP329 label import/export is an open pull request (#2712, opened 2026-09-11), not in a release. testnet4 is unsupported (#2516). On Windows with a remote Linux node, issue #1770 reports wallet-path separator problems. Specter-DIY firmware is a separate project (specter-diy). |

**Requires verification**

- Whether Specter-Setup-*.exe and specterd.exe carry Authenticode signatures was not checked (the electron-builder configuration contains no Windows signing settings).
- The per-user install location and the /S silent switch of Specter-Setup-*.exe follow electron-builder NSIS defaults and were not tested.
- Compatibility with Bitcoin Core 30.x and 31.1 is inferred from the descriptor-wallet code path and one issue report with Core 30.2 (#2624); upstream CI tests bitcoind 27.2.0 and no release note claims Core 30/31 support.
- Whether Jade Plus and BitBox02 Nova are detected over USB with the bundled HWI 3.1.0 (support for both was added in HWI 3.2.0) was not tested.
- The exact GitHub Container Registry image path of the official Docker image was not checked.
- The on-disk layout of wallet and device JSON files is inferred from the manager classes and not documented.
- The QR encodings (UR or others) used for each QR signer were not verified.
- Hidden-service behaviour: the FAQ says it is not supported in 2.0, while the 2.1.x code starts a hidden service with --tor; not tested.
- Whether the PyInstaller Windows build bundles libusb for HWI USB access was not checked (the pip instructions ask users to copy libusb DLLs into System32).
- That writing node JSON files and config.json while specterd is stopped is safe is inferred from the persistence code; Specter rewrites config.json at start-up. Not tested.
- The Windows minimum version is not stated upstream; Windows 10 is inferred from Electron 39.

| APIs and interfaces | `usb`: COLDCARD USB protocol over HID (ckcc-protocol): firmware version, chain (BTC or XTN), master fingerprint, xpubs, address display, PSBT upload and signing (approved on the device), message signing, encrypted backup, firmware upload and HSM mode. Link-layer encryption versions: v1 (legacy, default), v2, and v3 (authenticated, direction-separated keys and replay protection; opt-in, added in firmware 5.6.2/1.5.2Q and ckcc-protocol 1.6.0). ([documentation](https://github.com/Coldcard/ckcc-protocol/blob/master/PROTOCOL.md))<br>`file`: microSD and Virtual Disk. Exports: wallet files for Sparrow, Bitcoin Core (an importdescriptors command), Electrum and generic descriptors (single-sig with optional <0;1> multipath), XPUB export, multisig descriptors in 'pretty', bare and Bitcoin Core formats. Imports: COLDCARD multisig text files (Name:, Policy: M of N, Format: p2sh | p2wsh | p2sh-p2wsh, Derivation:, then one 'XFP: xpub' line per co-signer) or BIP-380 descriptors. Files saved to SD or Virtual Disk can be accompanied by a signature file. Cards must be FAT32 or FAT12. ([documentation](https://coldcard.com/docs/multisig/))<br>`qr`: COLDCARD Q only: scans PSBTs (Base64 or hex), finalised transactions, xpubs, BIP-21 URIs, addresses, multisig definitions in COLDCARD or descriptor format, SeedQR (not Compact SeedQR) and BBQr (files up to 2 MiB); shows signed PSBTs and exports as QR or BBQr. The QR documentation does not mention UR (BCR-2020-005). Mk4/Mk5 have no camera and can only display small QR codes (for example short multisig descriptors). ([documentation](https://coldcard.com/docs/qr-scanner/))<br>`nfc`: NFC tap (Mk4, Mk5, Q) to exchange PSBTs, signed transactions, addresses and xpubs with a phone (for example Nunchuk); also used for BSMS rounds and Key Teleport. | Security implications | July 2026 seed-generation incident (advisory published 2026-07-30, updated 2026-08-01): a firmware bug weakened device-generated entropy and attackers regenerated affected private keys offline and stole funds. Affected: Mk2/Mk3 firmware 4.0.1 to 4.1.9 (most severe); seeds generated on Mk4/Mk5 before 5.6.0, on Q before 1.5.0Q and on EDGE before 6.6.0X/6.6.0QX (about 72 instead of 128 bits). Updating does not repair an existing seed: such wallets must be migrated to a new seed unless at least 50 private, fair dice rolls were added. TAPSIGNER, OPENDIME and SATSCARD are stated to be unaffected. BTCortex cannot tell from an xpub which firmware generated a seed, so it must show the advisory and the minimum fixed release per track (5.6.0, 1.5.0Q, 4.2.0, 6.6.0X/6.6.0QX; recommended 5.6.3/1.5.3Q) whenever a COLDCARD is detected or chosen, and never offer to 'check' a seed. Firmware authenticity: the device only runs factory-signed firmware (red CAUTION LED until an upgrade is blessed, green GENUINE LED afterwards); downloads are verified with releases/signatures.txt, a SHA-256 list clear-signed by OpenPGP key 4589779ADFC14F3327534EA8A3A31BAD5A2A5B10 (Peter D. Gray, DocHex on Keybase; issuer confirmed from the 2026-09-30 signature). Recent hardening: SIGHASH_SINGLE blocked by default, re-verification of the staged PSBT before signing, rejection of duplicate inputs and negative amounts, authenticated USB encryption v3, removal of the unused USB serial interface, warnings before externally signed firmware or downgrades. BTCortex must never send passphrases or seed material, never enable HSM mode and never sign without the user approving on the device. |

| Notes | EDGE is a separate preview track (6.x 'X' builds that have 'not been qualified and tested to the same standard as a normal release'): Taproot since 6.0.0X, miniscript and MiniTapscript since 6.1.0X; BSMS (BIP-129; coordinator and signer roles, up to 15 signers, STANDARD, EXTENDED or NO_ENCRYPTION, files bsms_*.token, bsms_sr1*.dat/.txt, bsms_cr2*.dat/.txt) is documented as an EDGE-only preview. Coinkite's EDGE post names AnchorWatch, Liana and Keeper as miniscript/Taproot coordinators. Other features: COLDCARD Co-Signing (CCC), Single Signer Spending Policy (SSSP), Key Teleport between Q devices, Seed Vault, Trick PINs and Delta Mode, Codex32 and Shamir backups (5.6.3/1.5.3Q), PSBTv2 (5.6.3 adds per-input locktimes), BIP-322 signing. HWI device matrix, COLDCARD column: xpub retrieval, message signing, backup, P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH and P2SH/P2SH-P2WSH/P2WSH multisig inputs, non-wallet and mixed inputs, display on device; no setup, wipe or recovery through software; Taproot inputs not marked as supported. HWI master (unreleased; PR #849 merged 2026-08-20) adds EDGE handling and Taproot address display. |

Desktop coordinators therefore need a webcam or a microSD reader. Passport Prime pairs with the mobile Envoy app over QuantumLink (Bluetooth) and uses QR codes or transaction files with other wallets; its USB 'Airlock' storage is read-only by default after disconnection. |

Desktop coordinators documented by Foundation for Passport Core: Sparrow, Specter Desktop, Nunchuk and Keeper; also listed: Bitcoin Core, Bitcoin Safe, BlueWallet, Casa, Electrum, Fully Noded, Simple Bitcoin Wallet, Zeus; Bull Bitcoin connection flow added in 2.3.11. |

KeyOS 1.3.0 adds multisig configuration import via the crypto-output UR type (for Sparrow), single-part UR support and a universal QR scanner; Prime can export a multisig configuration (script type, threshold, co-signer xpubs) as a QR code or file. — authentication: Device PIN; every signature is approved on the device. ([documentation](https://docs.foundation.xyz/passport/connect/))<br>`file`: Passport Core microSD: PSBT files, wallet export files, multisig configuration files and firmware (.bin) updates; file hashes can be viewed on the device. Passport Prime: transaction files on external storage. ([documentation](https://docs.foundation.xyz/prime/connect/))<br>`other`: Passport Prime QuantumLink: encrypted Bluetooth link to Envoy for account sync, transactions and firmware updates (replay hardening in KeyOS 1.3.0). — authentication: Pairing with Envoy ([documentation](https://foundation.xyz/blog/keyos-version-1-3-0-is-now-available)) |

| Resources | — |

KeyOS 1.3.0 (2026-07-17) followed a third-party audit (kernel, cryptography, USB, NFC, QuantumLink, PSBT handling) and fixed, among others, AES-GCM counter reuse in partial-block streaming, encrypted eMMC proceeding with all-zero keys, unauthenticated RemoteUpdate payloads, plaintext hot-wallet key material in logs, and validation of PSBT inputs against attacker-supplied funding data. Passport Core has no USB data path, which removes a host attack surface. BTCortex must not use Prime's seed import, Vault or BIP-85 features. |

| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | Passport Core release assets: v<version>-passport.bin and v<version>-founders-passport.bin with SHA-256 and MD5 hashes. Passport Core is discontinued (no longer produced). Foundation states that Passport Core integrations do not automatically carry over to Prime; unlisted wallets should be confirmed with Foundation support. |

Each asset has a detached .asc signature and CHECKSUMS/CHECKSUMS.asc are provided, signed by the key 'Frostsnap <security@frostsnap.com>' (primary F19CCCCD876B6E57FB712206A9D5981F42B0EA50, signing subkey A0D99F559A2E20CFE6D18ABDFE2521845E568DAE). | APIs and interfaces | `usb`: Devices connect to the app (and to each other in a daisy chain) over USB-C for key generation, signing and firmware upgrades. — authentication: No device PIN; device secrets are encrypted with a key protected by the paired phone's secure element. ([documentation](https://github.com/frostsnap/frostsnap/blob/master/README.md))<br>`gui`: Frostsnap app (Flutter) acting as FROST coordinator and wallet; uses Electrum servers for chain data. ([documentation](https://frostsnap.com/)) |
| Command-line interface | — |
| Remote management | — |
| Node compatibility | The app acts as the coordinator and uses Electrum servers (v0.4.0 notes mention Electrum error reporting and testnet/signet servers). FROST keys produce single-key Taproot outputs, so a watch-only import elsewhere would be a tr() descriptor; v0.4.0 adds descriptor checksum generation. Interoperability with sparrow or bitcoin-core watch-only wallets was not verified. |

| Storage | — |
| Resources | — |
| Security implications | Threshold design removes the single point of failure of one device; keys are generated collaboratively with entropy from the phone or laptop. Devices have no PIN or secure element. v0.4.0 fixed a malicious-app attack that could get a device to sign an output hidden from its confirmation screen, and change addresses that could fall outside the recovery scan range; it also blocks firmware downgrades and publishes a deterministic firmware digest. FROST signing is not PSBT multisig: standard coordinators cannot co-sign, and recovery depends on Frostsnap's backup format. Young 0.x project without a published third-party audit. |
| Licence | MIT |
| Licence notes | — |

| Priority | P3 |
| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | Distinct from PSBT multisig: on chain a FROST wallet is a single Taproot key, which improves privacy and fees but ties recovery to Frostsnap's tools. |

### Ledger (Nano S Plus, Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | Hardware signing devices |

| Official repository | — |

The original Nano S stays on app 2.2.8 (nanos 2.1.0) and is no longer on the comparison page. Nano Gen5 announced 2025-10-23. |
| Superseded by | — |
| Latest verified stable release | Ledger Bitcoin app 2.5.1 (2026-09-09) — <https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md> |

| WSL2 | not-applicable |
| Docker | not-applicable |
| Other platforms | USB-C on all current models (Nano X and Nano S Plus ship a USB-A to USB-C cable); Bluetooth on Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex and Stax; NFC on Nano Gen5, Flex and Stax (comparison page). Android supports all models; the Nano S Plus 'does not work with iOS devices'. No QR or microSD signing. |
| APIs and interfaces | `usb`: APDU exchange over USB HID with the Bitcoin app open. Apps >= 2.1.0 use the new protocol with wallet policies (register_wallet returns an HMAC that the host must store and send with later signing and address-display requests); apps 1.x/2.0.x use the legacy protocol. The Bitcoin app reports its name and version; the master fingerprint and xpubs at standard paths are exported without confirmation (standard BIP-87 xpubs since 2.5.0). — authentication: Device PIN; on-device approval of policy registration, address display and signing. ([documentation](https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin/blob/develop/README.md))<br>`other`: Bluetooth LE (Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax), used by Ledger Wallet mobile; not used by HWI. — authentication: Bluetooth pairing confirmed on the device. ([documentation](https://shop.ledger.com/pages/hardware-wallets-comparison)) |
| Command-line interface | HWI: hwi enumerate (models ledger_nano_s, ledger_nano_x, ledger_nano_s_plus, ledger_stax, ledger_flex in 3.2.0; ledger_nano_gen5 only on master), hwi -t ledger -d <path> getxpub/getdescriptors/displayaddress/signtx. The Bitcoin app must be open on the device. |
| Remote management | None; local USB peripheral. |
| Node compatibility | Node-agnostic. HWI converts PSBTs to version 2 for the new app protocol and registers multisig wallets on the device during signing (requires the cosigners' xpubs in the PSBT global xpub field). Bitcoin Core can drive it through HWI as an external signer. |
| Dependencies | requires: [Ledger Wallet (formerly Ledger Live)](#entry-ledger-live) — Ledger Wallet (formerly Ledger Live) installs and updates the Bitcoin app and Ledger OS.<br>enhances: [HWI (Hardware Wallet Interface)](#entry-hwi) or [Sparrow Wallet](#entry-sparrow) or [Electrum](#entry-electrum) or [Liana](#entry-liana) or [Specter Desktop](#entry-specter-desktop) or [Nunchuk](#entry-nunchuk) — Host software that exports xpubs, registers policies, displays addresses and signs PSBTs. |
| Networking | None on the device; Bluetooth/NFC are local radio links. |
| Storage | — |
| Resources | — |
| Security implications | Secure element (ST33K1M5, CC EAL6+ on the Nano S Plus; Nano X listed as EAL5+); Ledger OS is closed source, the Bitcoin app is open source. Ledger Recover (opt-in, identity-based subscription service provided by Coincover) splits encrypted seed entropy into three fragments held by Coincover, Ledger and EscrowTech (two needed for recovery); its 2023 announcement was controversial because it showed that the firmware can export seed material when the user consents. BTCortex must never promote or automate it. Incidents: Ledger Connect Kit npm supply-chain attack on 2023-12-14 (malicious versions 1.1.5-1.1.7 of a web library live for about five hours; Ledger says it did not affect devices or Ledger Live) and the e-commerce/marketing database breach of 2020-06-25 (about one million email addresses, 9 500 postal details), which keeps fuelling phishing. Bitcoin app hardening: 2.4.6 rejects miniscript policies with meaningless older(n); 2.5.0 requires a persistent setting to sign non-standard sighash flags. BTCortex: verify addresses on the device, store policy HMACs per wallet, never ask for the 24 words. |
| Licence | — |
| Licence notes | Ledger OS is proprietary. The Bitcoin app (LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin) is Apache-2.0. |
| Integration mechanisms | Discover with hwi enumerate; show model (from the USB product ID), Bitcoin app version and fingerprint; ask the user to open the Bitcoin app if it is not running<br>Import xpubs/descriptors at standard BIP-44/49/84/86 and BIP-48/87 paths into watch-only wallets<br>Register multisig or miniscript policies on the device with explicit user approval and store the returned HMAC with the wallet<br>Display addresses on the device; sign PSBTs only after explicit user action<br>Launch Ledger Wallet for Ledger OS and Bitcoin app updates (close it before HWI sessions) |
| Feasible support levels | Connected Application, Research Only |
| Recommended support level | Connected Application |
| Implementation feasibility | high — HWI supports all current models except the Nano Gen5 in the 3.2.0 release (the Gen5 product ID was added on master). The Bitcoin app is the most capable mainstream signer for policies: wsh and Taproot miniscript, multisig up to 15 cosigners (2.4.0), musig() key expressions (2.4.0). BIP-388 policy signing through HWI's signtx was merged on master on 2026-08-25 and is not yet released. |
| Priority | P2 |
| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | The repository was renamed from LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin-new to LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin (the old URL redirects); the legacy app lives on as app-bitcoin-legacy. Unreleased changes on develop add BIP-322 message signing and make MuSig2 nonces independent of the transaction (only one pending signing session per policy). 'apex_p' is Ledger's build target name; HWI master maps product ID 0x80 to ledger_nano_gen5. Ledger announced a phone-like 'Ledger Atom' device on 2026-10-15 for reservation only (not verified beyond search results). |

| Notes | Model codes: T1B1 Model One, T2T1 Model T, T2B1 and T3B1 Safe 3 (two hardware revisions), T3T1 Safe 5, T3W1 Safe 7. HWI signing limits (hwilib/devices/trezor.py): multisig up to n-of-15; no arbitrary scriptPubKey/redeemScript/witnessScript; Taproot inputs cannot be combined with external inputs; Taproot needs Model One firmware >= 1.10.4 or Model T firmware >= 2.4.3; non-wallet inputs removed in firmware 1.10.6 / 2.4.4; no descriptor registration and no BIP-388 policy signing. Trezor Safe 7 specifications (trezor.io): USB-C, Bluetooth 5.0+, Qi2 wireless charging, 2.5-inch touchscreen, TROPIC01 + EAL6+ Optiga + STM32U5. A Bitcoin-only firmware build exists for every current model (url_bitcoinonly in releases.json). Trezor Suite coinjoin was discontinued in June 2024 (see trezor-suite). |

**Requires verification**

- Whether a running Trezor Suite (internal bridge) prevents HWI from claiming the USB interface on Windows was not tested; it is expected because only one process can claim a WinUSB interface.
- The Safe 3 and Safe 5 secure element is described by trezor.io only as 'EAL6+ certified'; the Optiga part name is taken from the Safe 7 page and was not checked for the Safe 3/5.
- Published physical seed-extraction attacks against the Model One and Model T (Kraken Security Labs, 2019-2020) were seen only in search results; the Kraken blog returned HTTP 403.
- Whether Sparrow's own hardware-wallet layer or Electrum's Trezor plugin already supports the Safe 7 (THP) was not checked in this part.
- The Model One connector type and Windows behaviour of very old Model One bootloaders in HID mode were not re-verified.

## Signing tools and bridges

<a id="entry-hwi"></a>

### HWI (Hardware Wallet Interface)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Category | Signing tools and bridges |
| Purpose | Python library (hwilib) and command-line tool from the Bitcoin Core organisation that gives one JSON interface to USB hardware wallets: enumerate devices, export xpubs and output descriptors, display addresses on the device and sign PSBTs. It is the reference external signer for Bitcoin Core's -signer option. |
| Official website | <https://hwi.readthedocs.io/> |
| Official repository | <https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI> |
| Maintenance status | maintenance-only — Release 3.2.0 on 2026-02-10 (3.1.0 on 2024-09-17, 3.0.0 on 2024-04-06). Latest master commit 2026-08-25 ('Optionally pass BIP388 policy to signtx', unreleased). Pinned issue #850 'Future of this repo' (achow101, 2026-08-18): no new features or device support except MuSig2, the next release 'will likely be the final release of HWI', then minimal maintenance and archiving once a replacement is ready; BHWI is named as a promising successor. Repository not archived. |
| Superseded by | — |
| Latest verified stable release | 3.2.0 (2026-02-10) — <https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI/releases/tag/3.2.0> |
| Verification date | 2026-10-21 |
| Native Windows | yes |
| Windows versions | — |
| Windows architectures | x64 |
| Windows distribution | Portable ZIP hwi-3.2.0-windows-x86_64.zip (60 113 236 bytes) containing hwi.exe (command line) and hwi-qt.exe (GUI), both PyInstaller builds; no installer. SHA-256 values for the ZIP and for both executables inside it are in SHA256SUMS.txt.asc (clear-signed). Also a Python wheel and source package (Python >=3.9,<3.13). |
| WSL2 | likely |
| Docker | no |
| Other platforms | Linux x86_64 and aarch64 tarballs (udev rules needed), macOS x86_64 and arm64 tarballs, PyPI package hwi. |
| APIs and interfaces | `cli`: hwi.exe [global options] <command>. Global options: -d/--device-path, -t/--device-type, -f/--fingerprint, -p/--password, --stdinpass, --chain {main,test,regtest,signet,testnet4}, --debug, --stdin, -i/--interactive, --expert, --emulators, --version. Commands in 3.2.0: enumerate, getmasterxpub, signtx, getxpub, signmessage, getkeypool, getdescriptors, displayaddress, setup, wipe, restore, backup, promptpin, togglepassphrase, sendpin, installudevrules. JSON results on stdout, prompts and debug output on stderr, errors as {"error": ..., "code": ...}. registerdescriptor and signtx/displayaddress --registration (BIP388 policies) exist only on unreleased master. — authentication: On-device PIN/confirmation; Trezor One and KeepKey use promptpin/sendpin with a scrambled matrix; BitBox02 needs a prior Noise pairing (done in the BitBoxApp when HWI runs non-interactively). ([documentation](https://hwi.readthedocs.io/en/3.2.0/usage/cli-usage.html))<br>`library-api`: hwilib Python API (commands.enumerate, find_device, getxpub, getdescriptors, displayaddress, signtx and others) with per-device HardwareWalletClient classes; device libraries are vendored inside hwilib. ([documentation](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/HWI/blob/3.2.0/hwilib/commands.py))<br>`usb`: Talks to devices directly over HID (hidapi), libusb/WebUSB (Trezor) and USB serial (Jade), without vendor bridges or companion apps. Supported in 3.2.0: Ledger Nano S, Nano X, Nano S Plus, Stax and Flex (Bitcoin app open), Trezor One, Model T, Safe 3 and Safe 5, BitBox02 and BitBox02 Nova, Coldcard, KeepKey, Blockstream Jade and Jade Plus, and the legacy BitBox01. Not supported: Trezor Safe 7 (mandatory THP, issue #775) and Ledger Nano Gen5 (master only). ([documentation](https://hwi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/devices/index.html)) |
| Command-line interface | Read-only and low-risk calls BTCortex can use: hwi.exe --chain main enumerate; hwi.exe -f <fpr> --chain main getdescriptors --account 0; hwi.exe -f <fpr> getxpub m/84h/0h/0h; hwi.exe -f <fpr> getmasterxpub --addr-type wit; hwi.exe -f <fpr> displayaddress --desc "<descriptor>" (the device shows the address). Signing only after an explicit user action and with the device's own confirmation: hwi.exe --stdin -f <fpr> --chain main, then send 'signtx <base64 PSBT>' on standard input (this is how Bitcoin Core's external signer calls it and avoids command-line length limits). Never call setup, wipe, restore, backup, togglepassphrase or signmessage on the user's behalf; --password/--stdinpass would pass a BIP39 passphrase and should be left to wallet applications. |
| Remote management | None; HWI is a local process that needs USB access to the device. Remote signing would require running HWI on the machine the device is plugged into. |
| Node compatibility | Node-agnostic. Output descriptors from getdescriptors (receive and internal lists for pkh, sh(wpkh), wpkh and tr where the device supports them, with key origins [fingerprint/purpose'/coin'/account']) can be imported into a Bitcoin Core descriptor watch-only wallet (createwallet with disable_private_keys=true, blank=true; importdescriptors with a timestamp no earlier than the prune height on pruned nodes). Bitcoin Core's external-signer integration (-signer=<path to hwi.exe>, wallets created with external_signer=true, RPCs enumeratesigners and walletdisplayaddress, send) runs '<cmd> enumerate', '<cmd> --fingerprint <fpr> --chain <chain> getdescriptors --account <n>', '<cmd> --fingerprint <fpr> --chain <chain> displayaddress --desc <descriptor>' and '<cmd> --stdin --fingerprint <fpr> --chain <chain>' with 'signtx <base64>' on standard input (src/external_signer.cpp at v31.1); the documentation requires HWI 2.0 or newer. Works with Core 30/31 because only descriptor wallets are involved. |
| Dependencies | optional: [COLDCARD](#entry-coldcard) or [Trezor (Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3, Model T, Model One)](#entry-trezor) or [Ledger (Nano S Plus, Nano X, Nano Gen5, Flex, Stax)](#entry-ledger) or [BitBox02 (BitBox02 and BitBox02 Nova, Multi and Bitcoin-only editions)](#entry-bitbox02) or [Blockstream Jade](#entry-jade) or [KeepKey](#entry-keepkey) — Devices driven by HWI 3.2.0 (see interfaces for model limits).<br>optional: [Bitcoin Core](#entry-bitcoin-core) — Watch-only descriptor import, PSBT funding (walletcreatefundedpsbt), finalisation and broadcast; or Core's own -signer integration.<br>conflicts: [Trezor Suite](#entry-trezor-suite) or [Ledger Wallet (formerly Ledger Live)](#entry-ledger-live) or [BitBoxApp](#entry-bitboxapp) or [Sparrow Wallet](#entry-sparrow) — Applications that hold the same USB interface or COM port. Close them before an HWI session (BitBox02 pairing is the exception: it must be done in the BitBoxApp first, which must then be closed). |
| Networking | No listening ports. Normally no network access; the Jade driver relays the PIN-server exchange (unlock) to Blockstream's PIN server over HTTPS, using the first non-onion URL, when the Python 'requests' module is available, otherwise the user must use QR PIN unlock or recovery-phrase login on the device. |
| Storage | About 60 MB for the Windows ZIP; PyInstaller executables unpack to a temporary folder at each start. No persistent state except what the caller stores. |
| Resources | Negligible; each call is a short-lived process (start-up overhead of the PyInstaller executable not measured). |
| Security implications | HWI never sees seeds; it relays requests that the device must approve on its own screen. BTCortex must still treat it as a powerful tool: setup, restore, wipe, backup and passphrase options touch seed management and must never be exposed; signtx must only follow an explicit user action, with the PSBT reviewed in BTCortex and on the device; displayaddress should be offered before a receive address is used. Release verification: SHA256SUMS.txt.asc is clear-signed by Ava Chow (achow101), RSA-4096 key 1528 1230 0785 C964 44D3 334D 1756 5732 E08E 5E41 (created 2015-03-05, expires 2027-08-21; the 3.2.0 signature from 2026-02-10 verified on 2026-10-21 with the key from bitcoin-core/guix.sigs builder-keys); 3.2.0 hashes: ZIP 2f1a5574647e3ce11b1a05feab2fcbbf17061937c970d321d7f4c28a7b6eca23, hwi.exe e068d91b664597425a8ead02d7b86a02ad6c4b72746c42961f58a58b08f9fd79, hwi-qt.exe 10300209bb1fb27a9c9eb1804ae4414de534c2028d55a57d8618835ba6822a9f. Verify the inner hwi.exe hash after extraction too. Device-specific limits: Trezor removed non-wallet-input signing (One firmware 1.10.6+, Model T/Safe 2.4.4+); Trezor has no descriptor registration; the published support matrix is partly outdated (it marks BitBox02 Taproot unsupported although the driver handles it). Do not reuse third-party copies of hwi.exe (for example the fork bundled by Nunchuk) for BTCortex's own integration. HWI's winding-down (issue #850) means new devices and firmware changes will not be followed; BTCortex must design its signer adapter so that HWI can be replaced (BHWI, vendor libraries, or delegation to Sparrow). |
| Licence | MIT |
| Licence notes | MIT; the ZIP may be redistributed, but downloading and verifying the official release at install time keeps the provenance check visible. Vendored device libraries carry their own licences (not reviewed). |
| Integration mechanisms | Download hwi-<v>-windows-x86_64.zip and SHA256SUMS.txt.asc from the GitHub release; verify the clear-signed checksum file against the pinned fingerprint 152812300785C96444D3334D17565732E08E5E41, then the ZIP hash and, after extraction, the hwi.exe hash<br>Extract to %LOCALAPPDATA%\BTCortex\tools\hwi\<v>\ (no installer, no elevation, no drivers)<br>Run hwi.exe as a short-lived child process from the sidecar with a timeout for read-only calls, no timeout but a user-visible cancel for calls that wait for device confirmation, and JSON parsing of stdout<br>Device discovery: hwi enumerate (type, model, path, label, fingerprint, needs_pin_sent, needs_passphrase_sent, error, code); poll only on user request or while a device dialog is open, never while Sparrow or a vendor app is using the device<br>Watch-only import: getdescriptors --account N, show the descriptors and fingerprint to the user, then createwallet (disable_private_keys, blank, descriptors, load_on_startup) and importdescriptors in Bitcoin Core with a timestamp no earlier than the prune height<br>Address verification: displayaddress --desc for receive addresses before first use<br>Explicit signing: walletcreatefundedpsbt in Core, user review in BTCortex, then hwi --stdin with 'signtx <psbt>', finalisepsbt and a separate, explicit broadcast step<br>Alternative: configure Bitcoin Core's -signer=<path to hwi.exe> so Core's own RPCs (enumeratesigners, walletdisplayaddress, send) call HWI<br>Keep the integration behind a signer-adapter interface so it can switch to BHWI's HWI-compatible binary or delegate to Sparrow when HWI stops receiving device updates |
| Feasible support levels | Fully Managed, Research Only |
| Recommended support level | Fully Managed |
| Implementation feasibility | high — A signed, portable x64 ZIP with a stable JSON CLI that Bitcoin Core itself uses as its external-signer reference; no drivers or bridges on Windows. Risks: HWI is entering minimal maintenance (no new devices: Trezor Safe 7 and Ledger Nano Gen5 are already unsupported in the release), multisig and policy registration are uneven across devices, and device contention with Sparrow or vendor apps must be managed. Recommended scope: discovery, xpub/descriptor import, address display and explicit signing for single-signature watch-only wallets; leave multisig coordination and device registration to Sparrow. |
| Priority | P1 |
| Implementation status | researched |
| In-app catalogue | Yes |
| Notes | 3.2.0 added Jade Plus and BitBox02 Nova support, testnet4 (--chain testnet4), Jade native PSBT signing and PSBT MuSig2 fields; it parses and writes PSBT versions 0 and 2. HWI does not report firmware versions in enumerate output (vendor apps and device protocols do; see the hardware entries). Ledger devices need the Bitcoin app open; app 2.1.0+ uses the new protocol with on-device multisig/policy registration during signtx. Coldcard, Ledger and Jade cannot be set up or recovered through software. Model strings include ledger_nano_s_plus, ledger_stax, ledger_flex, bitbox02_nova_multi and bitbox02_nova_btconly. Integration through Sparrow (which uses its own Lark library) is safer for end users than BTCortex driving vendor SDKs directly: one mature UI owns registration, address verification and signing, and BTCortex only handles PSBT files and watch-only data. |

([documentation](https://docs.corelightning.org/reference/get-started-with-your-reference))<br>`rest`: clnrest plugin: enabled by clnrest-port (3010 is common; the plugin disables itself without it), HTTPS by default (clnrest-protocol), on 127.0.0.1 by default (clnrest-host), certificates from clnrest-certs (by default the gRPC ones). Every RPC method is POST /v1/<method>; a Swagger interface and a Socket.IO notification stream are served on the same port. — authentication: A rune in the Rune header (createrune, showrunes); a read-only rune suffices for read methods and for notifications. ([documentation](https://docs.corelightning.org/docs/rest))<br>`grpc`: cln-grpc plugin on grpc-port with mutual TLS. — authentication: Client certificates generated by the plugin. ([documentation](https://docs.corelightning.org/docs/grpc)) |
| Command-line interface | lightningd and lightning-cli (JSON-RPC over the Unix socket). |
| Remote management | clnrest (HTTPS with runes) or cln-grpc (mutual TLS) for remote clients; node packages expose them. |
| Node compatibility | Bitcoin Core through the bcli plugin (bitcoin-cli), so a reachable bitcoind with RPC is required. |
| Dependencies | requires: [Bitcoin Core](#entry-bitcoin-core) — Through bitcoin-cli (bcli plugin). |
| Networking | Peers on 9735; clnrest and cln-grpc only when their ports are set. |

| Resources | — |
